position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: Kings facing each other with one square between them. Whoever has to move must give ground.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: Draw a square from the pawn to the promotion rank. If the king cannot step inside it, the pawn runs home alone.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The winning method in rook endgames. The rook goes to the fourth rank to build a bridge, and the king walks out from in front of its pawn.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The drawing method. The rook holds the third rank so the enemy king cannot cross, and only drops back to check when the pawn advances.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The rook sits behind the pawn, so every step the pawn takes gives the rook more room, not less.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: With the queens gone the king is a fighting piece, and the one standing nearer the middle is worth more.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: A famous draw. The bishop does not control the corner the pawn is running to, so the lone king simply sits there.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The bishop is stuck on the color of its own pawns, so the knight, which can use both colors, is the better piece.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: One connected group of pawns defends itself. Three scattered groups need pieces to babysit them.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: A passed pawn guarded by another pawn. No piece can ever take it, so it ties the other side down forever.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The passed pawn sits far from both kings, so the enemy king has to leave everything else to chase it.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: A pawn with no enemy pawn ahead of it or beside it, and a rook behind it to push it home.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: A file with no pawns on it at all. The rook that takes it first reaches the enemy position first.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: Two rooks on one file, one behind the other. They protect each other and hit twice as hard.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: Your pawn is gone from this file and theirs is not, so their pawn becomes a target that cannot run.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: More pawns than the other side on this wing, which is where a passed pawn will come from.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: The bishop on g2 behind the pawns on f2, g3 and h2 is a solid roof, as long as that bishop stays home.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: Doubled pawns cannot defend each other, so a rook on their file has a fixed target.

position.title: The idea on its own
position.note: This pawn cannot advance and no pawn can defend it, so it stays where it is and waits to be attacked.

game.note: Black's pawn on c6 has no pawn left to guard it, so Rubinstein lines both rooks up on the open c file and wins it.

game.note: White gives away a bishop on h7 to pull the king out of its little house, and the knight and queen chase it into the open.

game.note: The kings hide on opposite sides, so Fischer marches his g and h pawns like a wave to smash open the front of Larsen's castle.

game.note: Kasparov trades his strong rook for a knight so that White's pawns become broken and his bishop can stare all the way down the long diagonal at the enemy king.

game.note: Fischer pushes his f pawn like a crowbar to pry away the pawns in front of the black king, and then his rook walks right in on f6.

game.note: Fischer smashes a bishop into f7, the weakest square in the black camp, and the king has to step out where the knight on e6 traps his own queen.

game.note: Capablanca pushes his two queenside pawns at Black's three, and after they trade off Black is left with a lonely weak pawn on c6 for White to attack.

game.note: Andersson tucks his pawns onto a6, b6, d6, and e6 and coils his pieces behind them, then uncurls with the break d5 in the center.

game.title: Silman vs Filguth, San Francisco 1977
game.note: White parks a piece right in front of Black's lonely d5 pawn, trades off the pieces that gave it life, and then wins the pawn in the endgame.

game.note: The two black pawns side by side on c5 and d5 look strong, and the whole game is Fischer showing how to freeze them and then attack them.

game.note: Karpov trades off the bishop that guarded the dark squares around the black king, and those squares become holes that the white queen walks straight through.

game.note: Black's bishop is shut in behind his own pawns and can barely move, while White's bishop flies across the board to deliver the final blow.

game.note: The white knight lands on f5 right beside the black king, the queen on g4 both guards the knight and aims at g7, and the two of them together leave the king no safe square.

game.note: The bishop plants itself on f6 and the queen lines up right behind it on the long diagonal, so both pieces stare at g7 in front of the black king and the mate threat never goes away.
